solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Boss, between 4 and 6, is practically useless?

parts.note: a boss is the head of an organisation
entries 4 and 6 are both kinds of cloud, so being between them places you among the clouds

explanation.surface: A sneering remark about a manager who turns up mid-morning and is of no real use.
explanation.walkthrough: The numbers point to the answers at 4-down and 6-down, NIMBUS and CUMULUS, both clouds.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone dreamy and out of touch is impractical, so the idiom suits a person of little practical use.

clue.text: Maybe text from old flame results in expulsion from church

parts.note: a former partner is an ex
a text message is one example of a communication

explanation.surface: A message from a former lover gets someone thrown out of their congregation.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal exclusion from a church's sacraments and fellowship is what this ecclesiastical penalty is.

clue.text: River south of airless Scottish town getting less rainfall

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece south of another is written below it, so it comes after
the word splits into air plus less, telling us to drop those three letters from the town's name

parts.note: Airdrie is a town in North Lanarkshire, Scotland

explanation.surface: A weather comparison: a river near a stuffy Scottish town sees less rain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'airless' strips AIR from AIRDRIE, a town east of Glasgow, leaving DRIE; R goes below it.
explanation.definitionFit: A place with lower rainfall is drier, the comparative of dry.

clue.text: Sunrise introducing a small amount of atmospheric pressure — it could bring rain

indicators.note: the risen sun takes in the other letters, introducing them into its middle

parts.note: in a down clue the sun rising reads upwards, so the word sun is written bottom to top
a means one, written as the Roman numeral I
MB is the abbreviation for millibar, a small unit of air pressure

explanation.surface: A weather forecast: at dawn a slight pressure change may herald showers.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'Sunrise' means the sun read upwards; 'a' is the Roman one, and the pressure unit is the millibar. 'introducing' puts those inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A nimbus is a dark rain cloud, the kind that brings rain or snow.

clue.text: Precipitation in central parts of ridge heading north — outlook for short range

parts.note: hail is one kind of precipitation
taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue going north means reading upwards, so the middle letters run backwards
all of the word but its first and last letters

parts.note: a stance is a point of view or outlook

explanation.surface: A weather report: hail falls on a hill ridge as the outlook covers only the near term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'central parts of' takes IDG from RIDGE and 'heading north' turns it to GDI. 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Within calling range of a voice, so close by: the phrase names a short distance.

clue.text: Sky coverage increasing steadily — 50 per cent of country

indicators.note: half of the ten-letter word, its first five letters, is kept

parts.note: cumulating means building up gradually
US is the United States

explanation.surface: A statistic: cloud cover across half the nation keeps rising.
explanation.walkthrough: Half of CUMULATING is CUMUL; add US.
explanation.definitionFit: A heaped white cloud is one of the things that covers the sky.

clue.text: Trouble in new roles is common, perhaps

indicators.note: to trouble is to disturb, so the letters of new roles are stirred up

parts.note: is shortens to 's, giving S

explanation.surface: Difficulty taking on new roles is a common experience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trouble' rearranges NEW ROLES to OWNERLES, and S comes from 'is' shortened. 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Common land is open to all, and the 'perhaps' admits that as an example of something no single person possesses.

clue.text: Suffering such mal, trees died right away

indicators.note: suffering signals the letters are in a bad way and must be rearranged
away tells us to send the named letter out of the word trees

explanation.surface: Struck down by this illness, the trees perished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right away' removes R from TREES; 'Suffering' then rearranges SUCH MAL TEES DIED. 'Mal' is French for illness, so the whole clue also describes the disease.
explanation.definitionFit: A fungal blight spread by beetles killed millions of elms, so dying trees are exactly its effect.

clue.text: School ideology creating division

parts.note: an ism is a doctrine or ideology

explanation.surface: A school of thought whose beliefs split its followers.
explanation.definitionFit: A split within a group, especially a church, is a division.

clue.text: One's protected by one's … one's exemption

parts.note: one's read as one is, which a speaker would say as I'm

indicators.note: the first piece sits inside the second, sheltered by it

parts.note: one's as a possessive is the same as my when speaking of yourself
one is a unit, with the 's read as is

explanation.surface: A stuttering legal sentence about someone shielded by their own exemption.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word does three jobs: a number, a possessive and a contraction of 'one is'. The ellipsis marks the speaker's pause.
explanation.definitionFit: Being free from an obligation or liability is the same as an exemption from it.

clue.text: Joey maybe messes up at one-all, getting dismissed finally

parts.note: to mar is to spoil or mess up
taken as written

indicators.note: the last letter of the score phrase is sent off

parts.note: one is I, followed by all

explanation.surface: A cricket or football report: a player called Joey blunders at a level score and is sent off at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: A joey is a baby kangaroo, not a player's name. 'getting dismissed finally' drops the last L of IALL, leaving IAL. 'at' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A joey is a young kangaroo, and kangaroos carry their young in a pouch, an example of a pouched mammal.

clue.text: Phone enquiry to personnel department in Dortmund area?

parts.note: in text-message shorthand on a phone, R U stands for are you
HR, human resources, is the personnel department

explanation.surface: Someone rings up the personnel office to ask about a job in Dortmund.
explanation.walkthrough: The text-speak question R U HR? means 'are you human resources?'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dortmund lies in Germany's big industrial region of the same name, so the region is the city's area.

clue.text: Spice said to make an entrée

indicators.note: said signals that the phrase sounds like the word to be written

parts.note: to make an entrance is to come in

explanation.surface: A cooking tip: a certain spice is supposedly what makes a main course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrée' looks culinary but here means entry; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Cumin is a seed spice used in curries and Middle Eastern cookery.

clue.text: Popular benefit cut initially introduced to North East not doing anything?

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
the dole is unemployment benefit in Britain

indicators.note: the letter is put into the abbreviation, introduced inside it
only the first letter of cut is used

explanation.surface: A political jibe: a popular welfare cut in the North East and claimants sitting idle.
explanation.walkthrough: THE DOLE is British unemployment benefit. C, from 'cut initially', goes into NE.
explanation.definitionFit: Laziness or idleness is the state of avoiding any activity.

clue.text: Breakfast items that man will finish

parts.note: eggs are typical breakfast items
he'll is the contraction of he will

explanation.surface: A man promises to finish off the eggs at breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finish' is a paint finish, not completing a task.
explanation.definitionFit: A paint with a slight sheen is one kind of surface finish for walls and woodwork.

clue.text: Where Irish politicians are found covering Egypt thoroughly

indicators.note: the phrase goes round the other letters, covering them

parts.note: Irish lawmakers sit in the Dáil, the lower house of the Irish parliament
ET is the international vehicle code for Egypt

explanation.surface: Irish deputies examining Egyptian affairs in depth.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dáil Éireann is Ireland's lower house; ET goes inside IN DAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Treating something item by item, with every particular covered, is doing it fully.

clue.text: Fast stream for hire with a bit of roach in it

indicators.note: the letter goes inside the phrase for hire

parts.note: something available to rent is for hire

indicators.note: the first letter of roach is the bit taken

explanation.surface: An angler's ad: a fast-flowing river to rent, with roach in it.
explanation.walkthrough: A roach is a freshwater fish, which fits the river picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A violent rush of water is a fast-flowing stream.

clue.text: Where one's taken for intimacy — being single's best part?

definitions.meaning: someone drawn away from others for a private word is taken out of earshot
on a vinyl single record, the main track went on the A side, the B side being the lesser one

explanation.surface: Musings on private moments and whether being unattached is the best part of life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'single' looks like an unattached person, but it is a record.
explanation.definitionFit: One is drawn aside for a private word, and a record's lead track is on side A.

clue.text: Get off toboggan, perhaps, in flood

definitions.meaning: a luge is a racing toboggan

explanation.surface: Someone climbs off a sled straight into floodwater.
explanation.walkthrough: A punning definition: the prefix de- means off, so 'de-luge' is a made-up verb for leaving a luge.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy downpour or great flood, as in Noah's story, is the second meaning.

clue.text: Chain letter

definitions.meaning: armour of linked metal rings is chain ...
letters are post, collected as the post

explanation.definitionFit: Linked-ring armour and delivered post share one word.

clue.text: Runs by uncovered chicken coops becoming homes for vermin

indicators.note: by means next to, so the two pieces sit side by side

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

indicators.note: taking off the top letter uncovers the rest of the word

parts.note: battery cages are rows of hen coops in intensive farming

explanation.surface: Chicken runs next to open coops get overrun with rats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' looks like chicken runs but gives R. 'uncovered' removes B from BATTERIES; 'becoming' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A made-up word in the pattern of hatcheries: places where rats would live.

clue.text: Foolish character with what should be on top underneath and either side

indicators.note: in this down entry the dot sits under the letter instead of above

parts.note: the letter i is a written character

indicators.note: the dot's letters sit on either side of a second i placed inside them

parts.note: a lower-case i should have its dot above it
the letter i is a written character

explanation.surface: A silly person who gets things upside down and inside out.
explanation.walkthrough: Picture a lower-case i with its dot moved underneath, and another i put inside DOT so the dot is on either side of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as a modifier, the word means stupid or senseless, as in an idiot remark.

clue.text: Irish party with a bit of leg on show, it's rumoured

indicators.note: a rumour is something heard, so the phrase is spoken to give the name

parts.note: the shin is part of the leg, and to feign is to show or put on

explanation.surface: Gossip about a party where a woman showed a bit of leg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a link between SHIN and FEIGN.
explanation.definitionFit: Ireland's republican political party, historically linked with the IRA.

clue.text: One of four in a lavatory?

definitions.text: One of four in a lavatory?

indicators.note: the answer is one part of the run of words, so it is found inside them

explanation.surface: A question about one fitting among several in a gents' toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run through 'fo-UR IN A L-avatory', and a gents might well have four such fittings.
explanation.definitionFit: A wall-mounted fitting used by men in a toilet is one of a row of such fixtures.

clue.text: We're groaning with heat after a bit of a storm when cycling — sick of such problems?

indicators.note: the rearranged pair of words follows the other piece
the first two letters move round to the end

parts.note: thunder is part of a storm

indicators.note: a groaning thing is in distress, so the letters are disturbed

explanation.surface: People moaning in the heat after a storm, fed up with the weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cycling' moves TH from the front of THUNDER to the back: UNDERTH. 'groaning' rearranges WERE HEAT to EWEATHER. 'when' and 'of such problems?' add flavour.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means feeling ill, slightly unwell rather than seriously so.
